title: The core formula: what you want over what you have, times the volume
blurb: Use want ÷ have x volume for liquids and want ÷ have for tablets, with units matched first and rounding left to the end.
question: A person is prescribed 37.5 mg of an oral liquid. The bottle label reads 25 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given?

teach.h: One formula, most of the paper
teach.body: The want over have formula is: volume = (dose wanted ÷ dose in stock) x stock volume. For tablets it is simply dose wanted ÷ strength of one tablet. Plain English: work out what fraction of the stock dose you need, then take that fraction of the stock volume. It drives the oral, injection and many measuring items on Part A.

items.label: what you Want ÷ what you Have
the Stock volume the Have is in

steps.label: 1. Same units
steps.sub: W and H both mg (or g, micrograms)

items: Staff nurse Fatima Hussain has a prescription for 37.5 mg of an oral liquid. The label reads 25 mg in 5 mL.
x stock volume: 1.5 x 5 mL = 7.5 mL.
Sense check: she wants more than 25 mg, so more than 5 mL. 7.5 mL fits; she types 7.5 mL.

teach.h: The three classic errors (37.5 mg from 25 mg in 5 mL)

teach.body: If the prescription is in g and the stock in mg, convert first: 0.3 g = 300 mg. Converting to the smaller unit usually avoids decimals. W and H must be in the same unit, or the answer will be out by 1000.

teach.text: Rounding too early: in a weight-based dose, round only the final volume. 1.5 mg/kg for 64 kg is 96 mg; rounding that to 100 mg before dividing gives 4 mL instead of 3.8 mL from 50 mg in 2 mL. Keep full figures on the calculator until the last step.

head: If W is...
Then the volume is...
teach.caption: Tablet answers are usually 0.5 to 4; oral liquids 0.1 to 30 mL; injection volumes are usually a few mL, so a very large volume means re-check your working.

items: Volume = W ÷ H x stock volume; tablets = W ÷ H.
Put W and H in the same unit first.
W goes on top: inverting it is the commonest error.
Do not forget the stock volume when it is not 1 mL.
Round once, at the end, to the instruction.

summary: You can now apply want ÷ have x volume to liquids and injections and want ÷ have to tablets, match the units first, round only the final answer, and sense-check the result against the stock.

A.q: A person is prescribed 150 mg of an oral suspension. The label reads 100 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: 150 ÷ 100 x 5 = 7.5 mL. Sense check: more than 100 mg needs more than 5 mL.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: Right number, wrong unit: the answer is a volume.

A.q: You have a prescription for 60 mg by injection. The ampoule contains 80 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: 60 ÷ 80 x 2 = 1.5 mL. Sense check: less than 80 mg needs less than 2 mL.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 2 mL stock volume (0.75 rounds to 0.8).
whyNot.3: Right number, wrong unit: the answer is a volume.

A.q: A person is prescribed 1 g. The tablets are 500 mg each. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.1: Did not convert 1 g to 1000 mg before dividing.
whyNot.3: Converted 1 g to 100 mg; 1 g is 1000 mg.

B.q: A person is prescribed 2.5 mg by injection. The ampoule contains 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: Rounded to one decimal place; the question asks for two.
whyNot.3: Gave the dose in mg as the volume.

B.q: A person is prescribed 180 mg of an oral suspension. The label reads 250 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: 180 ÷ 250 x 5 = 3.6 mL. Sense check: less than 250 mg needs less than 5 mL.

whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

B.q: A person is prescribed 0.3 g of an oral suspension. The label reads 200 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Did not convert 0.3 g to 300 mg before dividing.
whyNot.2: Converted 0.3 g to 3000 mg; 0.3 g is 300 mg.

C.q: An adult weighing 64 kg is prescribed 1.5 mg/kg by injection. The ampoule contains 50 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: Dose = 1.5 x 64 = 96 mg. 96 ÷ 50 x 2 = 3.84, which is 3.8 mL to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Rounded the dose to 100 mg before dividing; round only at the end.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 2 mL stock volume.

C.q: A person is prescribed 62.5 micrograms by injection. The ampoule contains 0.25 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: Did not convert units: 62.5 ÷ 0.25 mixes micrograms with mg.
whyNot.3: Gave the dose converted to mg (0.0625) as the volume.

C.q: A person is prescribed 450 mg of an oral liquid. The label reads 125 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Right number, wrong unit: the answer is a volume.

reteach.title: What fraction of the bottle's dose?
reteach.question: If 5 mL holds 25 mg, how many lots of 25 mg are in 37.5 mg?

blocks.body: Ask how many "lots" of the stock dose you need: 37.5 mg is 1.5 lots of 25 mg. Each lot comes in 5 mL, so 1.5 lots is 1.5 x 5 = 7.5 mL. That is all the formula does: W ÷ H counts the lots, and x volume turns lots into mL.

blocks.text: If your answer is smaller than the stock volume while the dose is bigger than the stock dose, you have turned the fraction upside down.

explain.body: Divide what you want by what you have. Want goes on top.

test.q: A person is prescribed 40 mg. The stock is 100 mg in 5 mL. What is want ÷ have?

whyNot.3: Tenfold error the other way: 40 ÷ 100 is 0.4.

explain.body: Multiply the fraction by the volume the stock dose comes in.

test.q: Want ÷ have comes to 0.6 and the stock dose is in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

explain.body: Convert the prescription and stock to the same unit before dividing.

test.q: A person is prescribed 0.75 g and the stock is labelled 250 mg in 5 mL. What is the prescribed dose in milligrams, ready to use in the formula?

whyNot.0: Multiplied by 100; g to mg is x 1000.
whyNot.1: Multiplied by 10; g to mg is x 1000.
whyNot.2: Multiplied by 10000; g to mg is x 1000.

explain.text: Sense check: a dose bigger than the stock dose needs a volume bigger than the stock volume.

test.q: A person is prescribed 90 mg by injection. The ampoule contains 60 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
test.why: 90 ÷ 60 x 1 = 1.5 mL. More than 60 mg needs more than 1 mL.

whyNot.3: Tenfold error the other way: 90 ÷ 60 is 1.5.
